11:1.headline: Jephthah's mother: 'zonah' may not mean what it seems
11:1.body: Radak says she was Gilead's concubine, called זונה because she was not married to him with a marriage contract and betrothal. Ralbag says she came from another tribe and did not marry within hers. The Targum renders it פונדקיתא, 'innkeeper'.

sources.quote: בן פלגש גלעד היה ונקראת זונה לפי שאינה עם בעלה בכתובה וקדושין
sources.says: Radak says she was Gilead's concubine, called זונה because she was not with him by marriage contract and betrothal.

sources.quote: ולפי שלא נשאת לאחד מבני השבט קראה זונה
sources.says: Ralbag says she was called זונה because she did not marry one of the men of her tribe.

sources.quote: בַּר אִתְּתָא פּוּנְדְקִיתָא
sources.says: The Targum calls him the son of a woman who is a פונדקיתא.

11:2.headline: 'Another woman' is a polite word for the brothers' insult
11:2.body: Metzudat David says the brothers spared their father's honor and did not say 'prostitute'. Radak reads 'another woman' as meaning a concubine's son.

sources.quote: חסו על כבוד אביהם, ולא זכרו שם זונה
sources.says: Metzudat David says the brothers spared their father's honor and did not mention the word זונה.

sources.quote: ולפירושינו יהיה פי' לא תנחל לפי שהיה בן פלגש וזהו בן אשה אחרת
sources.says: Radak says that on his reading, 'son of another woman' means he was a concubine's son.

11:3.headline: 'The land of Tov': a good land, or a man named Tov?
11:3.body: Radak, Metzudat Zion and Ralbag all say טוב is the name of a man, the lord of that land. Metzudat Zion compares Ruth 3:13.

sources.quote: אדון הארץ היה שמו טוב
sources.says: Radak says the lord of the land was named Tov.

sources.quote: טוב. שם אדון הארץ, וכן מצינו (רות ג יג) אם יגאלך טוב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says טוב is the name of the lord of the land, and compares Ruth 3:13.

sources.quote: וישב בארץ איש ששמו טוב
sources.says: Ralbag says Jephthah lived in the land of a man whose name was Tov.

11:6.headline: Katzin versus rosh: prominent, but not the ruler
11:6.body: Metzudat Zion says קצין means a position of authority. Malbim says there is a difference between ראש and קצין. A קצין stands at the edge of the camp because he is prominent, even though he does not rule over them.

sources.quote: לקצין. ענין שררה, וכן (ישעיהו ג ו) קצין תהיה לנו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says לקצין means authority, as in Isaiah 3:6.

sources.quote: יש הבדל בין ראש וקצין, הקצין הוא העומד בקצה המחנה מחמת חשיבותו ומעלתו בגבורה, או בעושר או בחכמה הגם שאינו ראש ומושל עליהם
sources.says: Malbim says a קצין stands at the camp's edge for his standing in strength, wealth or wisdom, though he is not the head who rules them.

11:11.headline: Jephthah's 'words before the Lord': terms of rule, or prayers?
11:11.body: Rashi says all his words were the terms agreed between him and the elders. Malbim says he set how far his rule would reach. Metzudat David says they were his prayers and pleas.

sources.quote: אֶת כָּל דְּבָרָיו. הַתְּנַאי שֶׁבֵּינֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says 'all his words' were the condition between them.

sources.quote: התנה עמהם משפטי הראשית עד כמה תגיע ממשלתו
sources.says: Malbim says Jephthah set with them the rules of leadership and how far his rule would reach.

sources.quote: את כל דבריו. דברי תפלתו ותחנוניו
sources.says: Metzudat David says 'all his words' were his prayers and pleas.

11:23.headline: The word built on 'inherit' can mean 'drive out'
11:23.body: The root is ירש, 'inherit', but Metzudat Zion says הוריש here means driving out. Radak adds a rule: joined to מפני, 'from before', it means driving out. Otherwise it means giving an inheritance.

sources.quote: הוריש. ענין גירושין
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says הוריש means expelling.

sources.quote: הוריש. ענין גירושין כתרגומו דתריך וכן כל אשר הוא דבק עם מפני הוא לשון גירוש וזולתו הוא לשון ירושה
sources.says: Radak says הוריש means expelling, like the Targum, and that with מפני it is expulsion, otherwise inheritance.

11:24.headline: 'Chemosh your god': Moab's god, named with a sneer
11:24.body: Radak says Chemosh was Moab's god, and he did not save Moab's land from the Amorite king. Metzudat David and Ralbag say Jephthah says this in mockery.

sources.quote: והנה הוא היה אלהי מואב רק זה אמר לו אתה שואל הארץ שהיא ממואב ומלך האמרי לקחה ממואב ולא הצילו כמוש אלהיו
sources.says: Radak says Chemosh was the god of Moab, and the Amorite king took Moab's land without Chemosh saving it.

sources.quote: ואמר לו על צד הלעג הלא את אשר יורישך כמוש אלהיך
sources.says: Ralbag says Jephthah said this to him as mockery.

sources.quote: אשר יורישך כמוש. בדרך לעג אמר
sources.says: Metzudat David says he said it in a mocking way.

11:37.headline: Her 'going down on the mountains' has three readings
11:37.body: Rashi reads וירדתי as a word of wailing, like Isaiah 15:3. He also quotes a midrash: the mountains are the Sanhedrin, who might find a way out of the vow. Radak prefers the plain sense: Mizpah, where Jephthah lived, stood higher than the mountains.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן יְלָלָה הוּא, וְדוּגְמָתוֹ (ישעיהו טו:ג)
sources.says: Rashi says וירדתי is a word of wailing and compares Isaiah 15:3.

sources.quote: עַל הֶהָרִים. לִפְנֵי סַנְהֶדְרִין, שֶׁמָּא יִמְצְאוּ פֶּתַח לְנִדְרְךָ
sources.says: Rashi quotes a midrash that 'on the mountains' means before the Sanhedrin, who might find an opening for the vow.

sources.quote: והנכון לפרש כמשמעו כי המצפה ששם היה בית יפתח היה גבוהה על ההרים
sources.says: Radak says the correct reading is the plain one: Mizpah, where Jephthah's house was, stood high above the mountains.

11:39.headline: The 'chok' it became: a ban on such vows, or yearly mourning?
11:39.body: Rashi first reads it as a ruling that no one should ever vow this way again. He then offers a second reading, tying חק to the next verse and the yearly custom of the women. Metzudat Zion says חק means something fixed.

sources.quote: גָּזְרוּ שֶׁלֹּא יַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם עוֹד כֵּן
sources.says: Rashi says they decreed that no one should do this again.

sources.quote: וְיֵשׁ עוֹד לִפְתֹּר: וַתְּהִי חֹק בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל. מְחֻבָּר לְמִקְרָא שֶׁלְּאַחֲרָיו
sources.says: Rashi offers another reading, joining חק to the verse that follows.

sources.quote: חק. דבר קבוע
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says חק means a fixed thing.

12:5.headline: 'Ephrathite' can mean from Ephraim or from Bethlehem
12:5.body: Here the word means a man of the tribe of Ephraim. Radak notes it can also mean a man of Bethlehem Ephrath, as when David is called the son of an Ephrathite.

sources.quote: נקרא אפרתי אשר משבט אפרים ונקרא אפרתי אשר מבית לחם אפרת כמו ודוד בן איש אפרתי
sources.says: Radak says a man from the tribe of Ephraim is called Ephrathite, and so is a man from Bethlehem Ephrath, as in 'David, son of an Ephrathite man'.

12:6.headline: The password meant 'current', fitting for a river crossing
12:6.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion say שבלת is the river's current, so the test line was 'let me cross this current'. Radak cites a view that this word was chosen because the current ran right where the men of Ephraim crossed.

sources.quote: שִׁבֹּלֶת הַנָּהָר הַזֶּה אֶעֱבֹר
sources.says: Rashi says the test phrase was 'the current of this river I will cross'.

sources.quote: כן יקרא מרוצת המים, כמו (תהלים סט ג) ושבולת שטפתני
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says shibbolet is the rush of water, as in Psalms 69:3, 'the current has swept me away'.

sources.quote: וי״מ כי לקח מלת שבולת לפי שהיה שבולת הנהר במקום שהיו עוברים בני אפרים
sources.says: Radak cites some who say this word was used because the river's current was at the place where Ephraim was crossing.

12:6.headline: Ephraim said 's' for 'sh', like the French, says Radak
12:6.body: Metzudat David says the men of Ephraim said samekh where others said shin, and Rashi says they stammered. Radak adds that any word with shin would do, and compares the French, who also could not say shin.

sources.quote: כדרך האפרתים שאומרים במקום השי״ן סמ״ך
sources.says: Metzudat David says this was the way of the Ephraimites, who said samekh in place of shin.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיוּ מְגַמְגְּמִים בִּלְשׁוֹנָם
sources.says: Rashi says they stammered in their speech.

sources.quote: כן היו מנסין אותם בכל מלה שיש בו שי״ן והאפרתים היו קורין אותה סי״ן
sources.says: Radak says they could be tested with any word that has a shin, since the Ephraimites read it as sin.

sources.quote: אולי היה אויר ארצם גורם להם זה כמו אנשי צרפת שאינן מבינים לקרא השי״ן
sources.says: Radak suggests the air of their land may have caused it, like the people of France who cannot pronounce shin.

14:1.headline: Judah went 'up' to Timnah, Samson went 'down'
14:1.body: Genesis says Judah went up to Timnah, and here Samson goes down. Radak cites the sages: Judah rose in honor there, while Samson was shamed by what he did there.

sources.quote: יהודה שנתעלה בה כתיב ביה עליה שמשון שנתגנה בה כתיב ביה ירידה
sources.says: Radak cites the sages that Judah, who was raised up at Timnah, is described as going up, and Samson, who was shamed there, as going down.

14:7.headline: Did Samson talk to the woman, or about her?
14:7.body: Rashi, following the Aramaic, says Samson spoke to her family about her. Metzudat David says he spoke with her himself, to see if she was wise.

sources.quote: עַל הָאִשָּׁה, דִּבֵּר לִקְרוֹבֶיהָ, כֵּן תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן
sources.says: Rashi says he spoke to her relatives about the woman, as Jonathan translates.

sources.quote: שמשון עצמו דבר עמה, להכיר בה אם היא משכלת
sources.says: Metzudat David says Samson himself spoke with her to learn whether she was wise.

sources.quote: בעבור האשה שיתנוה לו או דבר עם האשה עצמה
sources.says: Radak gives both: he spoke on her behalf, so they would give her to him, or he spoke with the woman herself.

14:8.headline: A 'congregation' of bees
14:8.body: עדה is the word for a congregation of people. Metzudat Zion says the verse borrows it for a swarm of bees, the way Proverbs calls rock badgers 'a people'.

sources.quote: אסיפת דבורים, ואמר ׳עדת׳ בלשון שאלה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means a gathering of bees, and that עדת is a borrowed word here.

sources.quote: כְּנִיסַת דְּבוֹרִים
sources.says: Rashi, giving the Aramaic, says it means a gathering of bees.

14:9.headline: He scraped the honey out, like bread stuck to an oven
14:9.body: רדה here means to pull loose something that is stuck. Rashi compares the sages' word for peeling bread off the oven wall, since honeycomb sticks to the sides of a hive.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן הַבְדָּלַת דִּבּוּק שֶׁל כָּל דָּבָר הַנִּדְבָּק
sources.says: Rashi says the word means separating anything that is stuck, like bread stuck in an oven or honeycomb stuck to a hive.

sources.quote: וירדהו. ענין הלקיחה ממקום דבוקו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means taking something from where it is stuck.

sources.quote: הרדיה בדברי רז"ל לקיחת הפת ממקומו שנדבק שם בתנור
sources.says: Radak says the sages use the same word for taking bread from where it stuck in the oven.

14:15.headline: The seventh day of the week, or of the feast?
14:15.body: Rashi says it was the seventh day of the week, the Sabbath, which fell on the fourth day of the feast. Radak also allows the plain reading, the seventh day of the feast.

sources.quote: לִימוֹת הַשַּׁבָּת, וְלֹא שְׁבִיעִי לַמִּשְׁתֶּה, וְהוּא רְבִיעִי לִימֵי הַמִּשְׁתֶּה
sources.says: Rashi says it is the seventh day of the week, not of the feast, and it was the fourth day of the feast.

sources.quote: ויש לפרש ביום השביעי כמשמעו שביעי לימי המשתה
sources.says: Radak says one can also read it plainly as the seventh day of the feast.

14:18.headline: 'You plowed with my heifer': a farm word for prying
14:18.body: Metzudat says חרש means both to plow and to dig into a secret, so Samson calls his wife the heifer they plowed with. Malbim hears a second play: she did not keep quiet (החרישה), she told.

sources.quote: ולפי שמלת ׳חרישה׳ היא משותפת לחרישה ממש ולחתירת המחשבה, כינה אשתו בשם ׳עגלה׳ המלומדת לחרוש
sources.says: Metzudat David says חרישה means both real plowing and digging with the mind, so Samson called his wife a heifer trained to plow.

sources.quote: גם היא מענין חתירת המחשבה והעיון בדבר, כמו (משלי ג כט) אל תחרוש על רעך רעה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word also means scheming in thought, as in 'do not plot harm against your neighbor'.

sources.quote: רק אשתי היא עגלה בלתי מלומדה לחרוש, בה חרשתם, ולא החרישה רק הגידה
sources.says: Malbim says his wife was the untrained heifer they plowed with, and she did not keep silent but told.

14:19.headline: Stripped clothes paid as 'changes of clothes'
14:19.body: The verse pairs חליצות with חליפות, words one letter apart. Metzudat Zion says חליצות are clothes stripped off, as in 'pull off the shoe', and חליפות are named for being changed.

sources.quote: חליצותם. ענין שליפה, כמו (דברים כה י) חלוץ הנעל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means pulling off, as in 'the one whose shoe was pulled off', and notes clothes are called חליפות because they are changed.

sources.quote: מַלְבּוּשִׁים שֶׁחָלַץ מֵעֲלֵיהֶן
sources.says: Rashi says these are garments he stripped off them.

14:20.headline: Who befriended whom?
14:20.body: Radak reads it as the companion Samson chose for his wedding. Malbim reads it the other way: the man had been her friend, and she loved him before.

sources.quote: שלקח אותו שמשון לריע
sources.says: Radak says Samson took him as a companion.

sources.quote: וזה שאמר אשר רעה לו שהיה ריעו כי אהבה אותו מקדם
sources.says: Malbim says she had a bond with him: he was her friend, and she had loved him before.

15:4.headline: He turned the tails, not himself
15:4.body: Rashi points to the vowels. וַיִּפֶן would mean he himself turned. וַיֶּפֶן, as written here, means he turned something else: he turned the foxes tail to tail.

sources.quote: וַיִּפֶן, מַשְׁמַע הוּא עַצְמוֹ פָּנָה
sources.says: Rashi says vayifen means he himself turned.

sources.quote: וַיֶּפֶן, מַשְׁמַע הִפְנָה אֶת אֲחֵרִים
sources.says: Rashi says vayefen means he turned others.

sources.quote: מבנין הפעיל כי הוא בשש נקודות
sources.says: Radak says it is the causative form, as its vowel points show.

15:4.headline: A torch between two tails hints at the stolen wife
15:4.body: Malbim says the torch set between two tails was a message. Samson's wife had been given to his friend. Proverbs compares taking a neighbor's wife to carrying fire in one's lap.

sources.quote: רמז להם כי כן שמו לפיד בין שני רעים
sources.says: Malbim says it hinted to them that they had put a torch between two friends.

sources.quote: היחתה איש אש בחיקו
sources.says: Malbim cites 'can a man carry fire in his lap', said of one who goes to his neighbor's wife.

15:5.headline: Vineyards and olives, or an olive grove?
15:5.body: The Targum reads כרם זית as two things: vineyards and olive trees. Radak also offers one thing: an olive grove, called a כרם because the trees stand close together like vines.

sources.quote: וְעַד כַּרְמַיָא וְעַד זֵיתָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'and up to the vineyards and up to the olives'.

sources.quote: ויקרא כרם זית הזיתים הנטועים ביחד הרבה כמו שנקרא כרם הגפנים
sources.says: Radak says olive trees planted close together can be called an olive vineyard, the way vines planted together are called a vineyard.

sources.quote: פרדס מאילני זית
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is an orchard of olive trees.

15:8.headline: 'Leg on thigh': horsemen and foot soldiers, or men falling?
15:8.body: The Targum reads שוק על ירך as horsemen with foot soldiers. Metzudat David explains: the rider sits high like the thigh, the walker low like the leg. Radak also offers a picture of men fleeing and falling, legs tumbling over thighs.

sources.quote: פָּרָשִׁין עִם רִגְלָאִין
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'horsemen with foot soldiers'.

sources.quote: דימה את הפרשים רוכבי סוסים אל הירך
sources.says: Metzudat David says the horsemen are compared to the thigh.

sources.quote: כי הנס ונופל על פניו מתהפך שוקו על יריכו
sources.says: Radak says one who flees and falls on his face has his leg flip over his thigh.

15:8.headline: A cleft in the rock, or a crag jutting out?
15:8.body: Rashi reads סעיף as a hollow in the rock of Etam. Metzudat Zion reads it as a tooth of rock sticking out, borrowed from סעיף, the branch of a tree.

sources.quote: בְּנִקְרַת סֶלַע עֵיטָם
sources.says: Rashi says it means in the cleft of the rock of Etam.

sources.quote: הוא שן הסלע
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is a tooth of the rock.

sources.quote: והוא לשון מושאל מענף האילן הקרוי ׳סעיף׳
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word is borrowed from a tree's branch, which is called a se'if.

15:14.headline: Did the ropes melt, or only seem to?
15:14.body: Ralbag offers two readings. Samson was so strong that the ropes felt as if they melted, since he needed no effort. Or God truly weakened the ropes by a miracle, like flax burnt in a fire.

sources.quote: באופן שנדמה לו כאלו נמסו אסוריו מעל ידיו
sources.says: Ralbag says it seemed to Samson as if his bonds melted off his hands.

sources.quote: שהש"י החליש על דרך המופת העבותו' ההם
sources.says: Ralbag says it may be that God weakened those ropes by a miracle.

sources.quote: כאלו נמסו מעל ידיו העבותים
sources.says: Metzudat David says it was as if the ropes melted off his hands.

15:15.headline: A fresh jawbone, still moist
15:15.body: Rashi says טריה means moist, and that he saw a medical book call the fluid from a wound טריה. Radak adds that Arabic uses טרי the same way.

sources.quote: טְרִיָּה. לַחָה, וְרָאִיתִי
sources.says: Rashi says teriyah means moist.

sources.quote: וְרָאִיתִי בְּסֵפֶר רְפוּאוֹת שֶׁקּוֹרֵא לַלֵּחָה שֶׁיּוֹצֵא מִן הַמַּכָּה
sources.says: Rashi says he saw a medical book that calls the fluid coming from a wound by this name.

sources.quote: וכן יקראו לה בערבי טרי
sources.says: Radak says Arabic calls it tari.

15:16.headline: With a donkey's jaw, donkey-heaps of dead men
15:16.body: Samson plays on חמור. It means donkey, and it also means a heap. Metzudat David calls it one word falling on another, and Ralbag says Samson paired the words for wit.

sources.quote: בלחי של חמור עשיתי חמרים, והוא לשון הנופל על לשון
sources.says: Metzudat David says: with a donkey's jaw I made heaps, a play of one word on another.

sources.quote: ואמר חמור חמורתים לזווג שם עם חמור על צד הצחות
sources.says: Ralbag says he said 'chamor chamoratayim' to pair the word with 'donkey', as a witty play.

sources.quote: חמור חמרתים. צבור צבורים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means a heap, heaps.

15:17.headline: Ramat Lehi: where the jaw was thrown, or a high place?
15:17.body: Radak and Metzudat David say the name comes from the Aramaic for 'he threw', since Samson threw the jaw there. Ralbag says the place was high, a רמה, and so was called Ramat Lehi.

sources.quote: על שם שהשליך שם את הלחי, כי התרגום של ׳וישלך׳, הוא ׳ורמא׳
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is named because he threw the jaw there, since the Aramaic for 'he threw' is 'urma'.

sources.quote: ולפי שהשליך הלחי שם קראו רמת לחי
sources.says: Radak says because he threw the jaw there, he called it Ramat Lehi.

sources.quote: וידמה שהוא היה מקום גבוה ולזה ג"כ קראו רמת לחי
sources.says: Ralbag says it seems the place was high, and for that reason too it was called Ramat Lehi.

15:19.headline: Ein HaKorei: the spring of the one who called
15:19.body: Rashi and the Targum say the spring is named for Samson's prayer: it came because he called out to God. Ralbag reads עין as 'eye': God's eye was on the one who called to Him.

sources.quote: מַעְיָן שֶׁבָּא עַל יְדֵי זַעֲקַת הַקּוֹרֵא אֶל ה׳
sources.says: Rashi says it is a spring that came through the cry of the one who called to God.

sources.quote: עֵינָא דְאִתְיְהִיבַת בִּצְלוֹתָא דְשִׁמְשׁוֹן
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'the spring that was given through Samson's prayer'.

sources.quote: ששם היה עין השם אל הקורא לו שהוא שמשון
sources.says: Ralbag says there God's eye was on the one who called to Him, Samson.

16:1.headline: A prostitute, or the woman who kept the inn?
16:1.body: The Hebrew says זונה, usually a prostitute. The Aramaic Targum calls her an innkeeper, and Radak and Ralbag follow it: Samson came to her house to spend the night.

sources.quote: וַחֲזָא תַמָן אִתְּתָא פּוּנְדְקִיתָא
sources.says: The Targum says he saw there a woman who kept an inn.

sources.quote: אשה זונה. איתתא פונדקיתא וכבר כתבנו דעת המתרגם בענין רחב הזונה
sources.says: Radak gives the Targum's 'innkeeper' and notes the Targum read Rahab the same way.

sources.quote: וראה שם אש' פונדקיתא ובא לביתה ללון שם
sources.says: Ralbag says he saw an innkeeper there and came to her house to sleep.

16:2.headline: They kept silent all night, or they plotted all night
16:2.body: The root חרש can mean to be silent, or to plot, as in 'do not plot evil'. Metzudat Zion gives both, and Radak says they acted deaf so Samson would not be on guard.

sources.quote: ענין שתיקה, כמו (במדבר ל ה) והחריש לה, או הוא מענין חתירת המחשבה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means keeping silent, or else digging out a plan.

sources.quote: או כל הלילה חשבו מחשבות איך להמיתו
sources.says: Metzudat David's second reading is that all night they thought up ways to kill him.

sources.quote: עשו עצמן כחרשים כדי שלא ישמר מהם שמשון
sources.says: Radak says they made themselves like deaf men so Samson would not guard himself from them.

16:3.headline: The grammar shows how easily he carried the gates
16:3.body: The plain form of this verb normally means to travel, not to move something. Malbim says it is used on purpose: Samson simply walked off, and the gates went with him.

sources.quote: ומלת ויסעם שהוא יוצא מן הקל מורה שע"י נסיעתו בעצמו הסיע גם אותם
sources.says: Malbim says the light form of the verb shows that by traveling himself he moved the gates too.

sources.quote: ויסע עמם ועם הבריח כי לא נמצא ממנו מפעל הקל יוצא כי אם בודד
sources.says: Radak reads it as 'he traveled with them and with the bar', because this form almost never takes an object.

16:4.headline: Her name says what she did to his strength
16:4.body: Malbim quotes the sages, who read דלילה as 'she weakened', from דלדל: she drained his strength, his deeds and his heart. He also notes that she kept her foreign name.

sources.quote: וחז"ל דרשו דלדלה כחו ומעשיו ולבו
sources.says: Malbim says the sages read the name as 'she weakened his strength, his deeds and his heart'.

sources.quote: אבל זו לא נתגיירה ונשאר שמה דלילה
sources.says: He adds that, unlike Samson's first wife, she did not convert, so her name stayed Delilah.

16:9.headline: A thread that snaps when it only smells the fire
16:9.body: The verse says the thread breaks when it 'smells' fire. Radak and Metzudat David say this means it snaps just from being near the flame, before the fire really touches it.

sources.quote: שינתק בהיותו קרוב לאש שלא ישלוט בו האש אלא מעט בריח
sources.says: Radak says it snaps when it is near the fire, which only reaches it a little, by smell.

sources.quote: כשהוא קרוב אל האש ורק מריח את האש, והוא מלשון מליצה
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is close to the fire and only smells it, a figure of speech.

16:13.headline: Locks of hair, named for being replaced
16:13.body: Metzudat Zion says מחלפות are the locks of hair on the head. They get this name from חלף, 'to replace', because they grow back after they are cut.

sources.quote: הם קווצות ותלתלי שער הראש, ועל כי יוחלפו בהתגלחם יקראו מחלפות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says they are the locks of the head, called מחלפות because they are replaced when shaved.

sources.quote: מַחְלְפוֹת. קְוֻצּוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says they are locks of hair.

16:17.headline: 'Like any man' now, not 'like one man' as before
16:17.body: Twice before, Samson said he would be 'like one of men'. Malbim says that meant one special strong man, so it was not quite a lie. Now he says 'like all men', the weak ones, and this time it is the truth.

sources.quote: והנה בפעמים הראשונים אמר והייתי כאחד האדם, ועתה אמר והייתי ככל האדם, כי נשמר מלדבר שקר
sources.says: Malbim notes the change from 'like one of men' to 'like all men', and says Samson was careful not to lie.

sources.quote: ועתה אמר ככל האדם, החלשים
sources.says: He says 'like all men' means like the weak.

16:18.headline: Written 'to her', read 'to me'
16:18.body: The written text says לה, 'to her', but it is read לי, 'to me'. Radak says the written form is what the messenger said to the Philistine lords, and the read form is what Delilah told the messenger.

sources.quote: לה כתיב וקרי לי והכתיב דברי השליח שאמר לסרני פלשתים והקרי דבריה שצותה לשליח
sources.says: Radak says the written 'to her' is the messenger's words to the lords, and the read 'to me' is her words to the messenger.

16:20.headline: How could he not know? He had just told her
16:20.body: Samson himself had said his strength would leave if he was shaved. Radak asks how the verse can say he did not know, and answers that he was half asleep, or that he knew his strength was gone but not that God had left him.

sources.quote: והלא הגיד לה כל לבו ודעתו היה כאשר יגלח יסור כחו ממנו
sources.says: Radak asks: did he not tell her all his heart, knowing his strength would leave if he were shaved?

sources.quote: ידע שסר ממנו כחו אבל לא ידע כי ה' סר מעליו
sources.says: One answer: he knew his strength had left him, but not that God had left him.

16:21.headline: Grinding grain in prison, or a word for sex?
16:21.body: Plainly, Samson ground grain at the prison mill, as Radak says prisoners did. Rashi notes the sages read 'grinding' as a word for sex, and Radak rejects that reading as far-fetched.

sources.quote: בָּרֵחַיִם, מְלָאכָה כְּבֵדָה וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ (סוטה י א) פֵּרְשׁוּ מַה שֶּׁפֵּרְשׁוּ
sources.says: Rashi says he ground with millstones, hard work, and that the sages gave their own reading.

sources.quote: רַבּוֹתֵינוּ פֵּרְשׁוּהוּ (במדבר רבה ט:כד) לְשׁוֹן תַּשְׁמִישׁ, כְּמוֹ ״וַיְהִי טוֹחֵן בְּבֵית הָאֲסוּרִין״
sources.says: Rashi says the sages read 'grinding' as a word for sex, as in Samson grinding in prison.

sources.quote: ודרך הדרש רחוק בזה
sources.says: Radak says the sages' reading is far from the plain sense here.

16:25.headline: They wanted him to laugh; he only performed
16:25.body: The crowd asks that Samson ישחק, laugh and be merry with them, but the verse says he ויצחק, made sport. Malbim says the first means the person is happy himself, the second does not, so Samson entertained them without joy.

sources.quote: השחוק הנרדף עם צחוק, נבדל ממנו במה שהשחוק מורה שהשוחק בעצמו י"ל שמחה לא כן המצחק
sources.says: Malbim says שחוק means the one laughing is happy himself, while מצחק does not.

sources.quote: אבל באמת שמשון רק צחק ולא שחק
sources.says: He says Samson in fact only performed and did not laugh.

16:26.headline: 'Let me feel the pillars', written two ways
16:26.body: The written and the read forms come from two different roots. Rashi reads it as feeling with the hands, like Isaac feeling Jacob. Radak's own reading is 'bring me close to the pillars'.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ (בראשית כז:יב): ״אוּלַי יְמֻשֵּׁנִי״
sources.says: Rashi compares Jacob's fear in Genesis 27:12 that his father will feel him.

sources.quote: והימשני. כתיב שרשו ימש והמישני קרי שרשו מוש והענין אחד
sources.says: Radak says the written form has the root ימש and the read form the root מוש, with the same meaning, and he takes it as moving toward something.

sources.quote: וי"מ אותו ענין מישוש וכן תירגם יונתן ואמישני
sources.says: Radak says some read it as touching, and the Targum translates it that way.

16:28.headline: Revenge for one eye now, the other saved for later
16:28.body: Why does Samson ask for revenge for only one of his two eyes? Rashi says he asked to be paid for one eye in this world and to keep the reward for the other for the world to come.

sources.quote: וּשְׂכַר עַיִן הַשֵּׁנִית הַנַּח לִי לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
sources.says: Rashi says Samson asked that the reward for the second eye be kept for him in the world to come.

sources.quote: תן לי שכר עיני אחת בעוה"ז ושכר עיני אחרת תהא שמורה לי
sources.says: Radak brings the same teaching: give me the reward for one eye in this world, and keep the other for me.

16:29.headline: He said he would lean; he pushed with all his strength
16:29.body: Samson told the boy he wanted to rest against the pillars, using שען. Malbim says the verse switches to סמך, which means pressing with all one's strength, and that is what he did.

sources.quote: שהסמיכה הוא בכל כחו
sources.says: Malbim says סמיכה means leaning with all one's strength.

sources.quote: ולכן להנער אמר ואשען עליהם, ובאמת ויסמך בכל כחו
sources.says: He says Samson told the boy 'I will lean', but in truth pressed with all his strength.

19:2.headline: Was she unfaithful, or did she just walk out?
19:2.body: ותזנה usually means she was unfaithful, and Radak allows that reading. But Metzudat Zion reads it as turning away from him, and Malbim says the sages held she did not sleep with another man, only crossed him.

sources.quote: בזתה אותו ויצאה מביתו והלכה לבית אביה או יהיה פירושו זנות כמשמעו
sources.says: Radak gives the Targum's reading, that she scorned him and left for her father's house, or else the plain sense of unfaithfulness.

sources.quote: ותזנה. עניינו הסרה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word here means turning away.

sources.quote: וזה מורה כדעת חז"ל (גיטין ו ב) שלא זנתה ורק עשתה נגדו דבר שלא לרצונו
sources.says: Malbim says the wording supports the sages' view that she was not unfaithful, but only did something against his wishes.

19:2.headline: Four months, or a year and four months?
19:2.body: Metzudat Zion and Radak say ימים, 'days', can mean a full year, as in Leviticus 25:29, so she stayed a year and four months. Radak also allows that the 'days' were just the four months.

sources.quote: ימים. שנה, כמו (ויקרא כח כט) ימים תהיה גאולתו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says 'days' here means a year, as in the law of redeeming a house.

sources.quote: ופי' ימים שנה או יהיה ד' חדשים פי' ימים
sources.says: Radak says 'days' means a year, or else the four months are what 'days' refers to.

sources.quote: שעמדה שם שנה וארבעה חדשים
sources.says: Ralbag says she stayed there a year and four months.

19:3.headline: Written 'to bring him back', read 'to bring her back'
19:3.body: The written word is להשיבו, to bring him back, but it is read להשיבה, to bring her back. Radak says the written form means he would bring himself back to her, and she would come back to him.

sources.quote: להשיבו. כן כתיב וקרי להשיבה ופירש הכתוב להשיבו אליה והיא תשוב אליו
sources.says: Radak says it is written 'to bring him back' and read 'to bring her back', and the written form means he would return to her and she to him.

19:5.headline: Prop up your heart: why a meal is called סעודה
19:5.body: Metzudat Zion says סעד means to prop up or support. A meal is called סעודה because it props up a weak heart, as in Psalms 104:15, 'bread sustains a person's heart'.

sources.quote: ועל שם זה יקרא האכילה סעודה, כי סועד ושוען את הלב מחולשתו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says eating is called סעודה because it supports the heart in its weakness.

sources.quote: לבל יחלוש הלב, סעד אותו באכילת פת לחם
sources.says: Metzudat David says: so your heart does not grow weak, support it by eating some bread.

19:9.headline: 'The day's camping': nightfall, or the stop you must make anyway?
19:9.body: Rashi and Radak read חנות היום as evening, when travelers stop for the night. Metzudat David reads it as the stop the Levite will have to make today anyway, so better to make it here.

sources.quote: עֵת שֶׁכָּל הוֹלְכֵי דְרָכִים נוֹטִים לַחֲנוֹת בַּבַּיִת
sources.says: Rashi says it is the time when all travelers turn in to stay at a house.

sources.quote: הלילה הוא חנות היום כי ביום אדם הולך הנה והנה ובלילה חונה
sources.says: Radak says night is the day's camping, since by day people move about and at night they rest; or it is the sun that seems to rest.

sources.quote: החניה אשר בהכרח תעשה היום, הלא טוב יותר לחנות וללון פה
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means the stop you must make today anyway: is it not better to stop and sleep here?

19:19.headline: 'Your servants': the old man's servants, or the Levite himself?
19:19.body: Radak first reads עבדיך as the old man's own servants, who could share the travelers' food. Then, with the Targum, he reads it as the Levite and his concubine politely calling themselves 'your servants'.

sources.quote: וי"ת ולעולימא דעם עבדך אמר עבדך על האיש ופלגשו כלומר הנער אשר עמנו ונכון הוא
sources.says: Radak says that by the Targum's reading, 'your servants' means the man and his concubine, so 'the lad with your servants' is the lad traveling with them, and he calls this correct.

sources.quote: ואת עצמו ופילגשו קרא עבדיו בדרך המוסר
sources.says: Metzudat David says he politely called himself and his concubine the old man's servants.

19:21.headline: Feeding the donkeys: a word from mixing grain into straw
19:21.body: Rashi reads ויבל as giving the donkeys יבול, produce. Radak and Metzudat Zion take it from בלל, to mix, because animal feed was grain mixed with straw, called בליל.

sources.quote: וַיִּתֵּן יְבוּל לַחֲמוֹרִים
sources.says: Rashi says he gave produce to the donkeys.

sources.quote: שרשו בלל רוצה לומר נתן להם מספוא והמספוא נקרא בליל
sources.says: Radak says the root is בלל: he gave them fodder, and fodder is called בליל because grain is mixed in with the straw.

sources.quote: הוא מלשון בלבול וערבוב, כי הדרך לבלול תבואה במספוא
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from mixing, because grain is usually mixed into the fodder.

19:22.headline: בליעל: people 'without the yoke' of heaven
19:22.body: Metzudat Zion splits the word into בלי עול, 'without a yoke', meaning men who have thrown off heaven's rule. The Targum likewise calls them 'men of wickedness'.

sources.quote: בליעל. בלי עול שמים, רוצה לומר, רשעים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says בליעל means without the yoke of heaven, that is, wicked.

sources.quote: גַבְרִין בְּנֵי רִשְׁעָא
sources.says: The Targum calls them men of wickedness.

19:22.headline: 'Let us know him': rape, or murder?
19:22.body: Rashi reads 'know' as sexual, as in Sodom. Radak notes the Levite later says they meant to kill him, so 'know' may mean kill, or the talk of killing may be a polite cover for the shameful act.

sources.quote: וְנֵדָעֶנּוּ. מִשְׁכַּב זָכוּר
sources.says: Rashi says it means lying with a male.

sources.quote: וי"ל כי היו רוצים להרגו כמו שספר הוא אותי דמו להרוג
sources.says: Radak says one could read it as wanting to kill him, as the Levite later reports, or that he used the word killing to cover the ugly act.

19:22.headline: Knocking, pounding, or only pretending to knock?
19:22.body: Metzudat Zion reads it as gentle knocking, and the Targum as pushing to break the door down. Malbim says the verb's form shows a show of knocking, not a real attack as in Sodom.

sources.quote: ענין הכאה בנחת על הדלת
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means knocking gently on the door.

sources.quote: דַחֲקִין לְמִתְבַּר דָשָׁא
sources.says: The Targum says they were pushing to break the door.

sources.quote: ולכן כתיב מתדפקים על הדלת בבנין התפעל, שמורה על הפעולה המדומה
sources.says: Malbim says the reflexive form shows a pretended action: they seemed to knock, but did not really, unlike Sodom where they came to break the door.

19:22.headline: They surrounded the house, not 'against' it as in Sodom
19:22.body: In Sodom the men surrounded 'against' Lot's house, to fight the host. Malbim says here they only surrounded the house to stop the guest slipping away, which is why they did not want the old man's daughter.

sources.quote: ופה כתיב נסבו את הבית, לשמור בל יברח האורח, לא שנסבו על הבית ללחום
sources.says: Malbim says here it is written they surrounded the house, to keep the guest from fleeing, not that they surrounded it to fight.

19:26.headline: Her husband is called 'her master'
19:26.body: Metzudat David says אדוניה, her master, means her husband. He is called master because she was his concubine.

sources.quote: הוא הבעל, ולפי שהיתה לו לפילגש, יחשב לאדון לה
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is the husband, counted as her master because she was his concubine.

3:8.headline: 'Rishatayim' may mean 'double wickedness', or be a place
3:8.body: Radak says it was his name, but that רשעתים may be a place, and he cites a midrash that reads it as 'two wickednesses', Balaam's and Kushan's. Targum Jonathan calls him כושן חייבא, 'Kushan the guilty'.

sources.quote: ביד כושן רשעתים. כך היה שמו ואפשר כי רשעתים שם מקום ובדרש מהו רשעתים על שני רשעיות שהרשיעו ארם לישראל אחת של בלעם ואחת של כושן
sources.says: Radak says it was his name, perhaps רשעתים is a place, and a midrash says it means two wickednesses done by Aram to Israel, one of Balaam and one of Kushan.

sources.quote: בְּיַד כּוּשַׁן חַיָבָא מַלְכָּא דַאֲרָם
sources.says: Targum Jonathan renders the name as Kushan the guilty, king of Aram.

3:10.headline: The 'spirit of the Lord' on Othniel: prophecy, strength, or wisdom?
3:10.body: Targum Jonathan reads רוח as a spirit of prophecy, and Ralbag allows prophecy or a share of the holy spirit. Radak reads it as a spirit of strength and courage, and Metzudat David as a stirring of wisdom to judge and courage to fight.

sources.quote: וּשְׁרַת עֲלוֹהִי רוּחַ נְבוּאָה מִן קֳדָם יְיָ
sources.says: Targum Jonathan says a spirit of prophecy from before the Lord rested on him.

sources.quote: ואפשר שיהיה זה נבואה או היה חלק מה מרוח הקדש
sources.says: Ralbag says it may have been prophecy, or a share of the holy spirit.

sources.quote: ויתכן לפרש רוח הכח והגבורה כי התעורר בגבורה להלחם עם כושן
sources.says: Radak says it can be read as a spirit of strength and might, since he was stirred to fight Kushan.

sources.quote: התעוררות חכמה לשפוט ואמיץ לבב להלחם
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means a stirring of wisdom to judge and courage to fight.

3:12.headline: God 'strengthened' Eglon, who was weak on his own
3:12.body: Metzudat David says Eglon was weak, and God made him strong against Israel because of their sins. Malbim says that by nature Israel would have beaten him.

sources.quote: חלש היה, וה׳ חזקו על ישראל בעבור מעשיהם הרעים
sources.says: Metzudat David says Eglon was weak and God strengthened him over Israel because of their evil deeds.

sources.quote: שעגלון היה חלוש מצד עצמו, ובדרך הטבע היו הם מתגברים עליו
sources.says: Malbim says Eglon was weak by himself, and by nature Israel would have overcome him.

3:15.headline: 'Left-handed' literally means 'shut': his right hand was closed
3:15.body: אטר comes from a verb for shutting, as in 'let the pit not shut its mouth on me'. Rashi, Metzudat Zion and Radak say his right hand was closed, meaning he could not use it, so he used his left.

sources.quote: אָטוּם בְּיַד יְמִינוֹ, שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה שׁוֹלֵט בָּהּ
sources.says: Rashi says אטר means shut, shut in his right hand, which he could not control.

sources.quote: כאלו יד ימינו סגורה, כי לא שלט בה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means as if his right hand were closed, since he had no control of it.

sources.quote: סגור יד ימינו שלא היה שולט בה והיה שמאליי והוא מן ואל תאטר עלי באר פיה
sources.says: Radak says it means his right hand was shut so he could not use it and he was left-handed, from 'let the pit not shut its mouth on me'.

3:19.headline: 'The idols' may be 'the quarries'
3:19.body: פסילים usually means carved idols. Rashi and Metzudat Zion say it is the place where stones are cut and smoothed, and Ralbag allows either a stone quarry or the idols of Moab.

sources.quote: מָקוֹם שֶׁפּוֹסְלִים שָׁם אֲבָנִים מִן הָהָר, וְכֵן תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן: מִן מַחְצְבַיָּא
sources.says: Rashi says it is the place where stones are cut from the mountain, and Targum Jonathan renders it 'from the quarries'.

sources.quote: הפסילים. מקום שמחליקים שם פני האבנים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the place where the faces of stones are smoothed.

sources.quote: עד שעבר מקום פיסלי האבנים או יהיה פירוש הפסילים פסילי אלהי מואב
sources.says: Ralbag says it is the place of the stone-cutters, or it may mean the carved images of Moab's gods.

3:19.headline: 'Hush!' is Eglon's: to his men, or to Ehud?
3:19.body: Rashi and Ralbag say Eglon told his attendants to be quiet, and Rashi adds that Targum Jonathan renders it 'go out'. Metzudat David and Radak say he told Ehud to say nothing until the attendants had left.

sources.quote: אָמַר עֶגְלוֹן: שִׁתְקוּ אֶת הַכֹּל מֵעָלַי, וְיוֹנָתָן תִּרְגֵּם הָס: סְלִיק, הוֹצִיא כָּל אִישׁ
sources.says: Rashi says Eglon said 'silence everyone around me', and Targum Jonathan renders הס as 'go up, remove everyone'.

sources.quote: ואמר המלך לעומדים לפניו הם רצה לומר שישתתקו עד שיצאו מעליו כל העומדים עליו
sources.says: Ralbag says the king told those standing before him to be silent until they all went out.

sources.quote: כאומר, אם דבר סתר הוא בפני בני עמך, שתוק ולא תדבר באזני העומדים מבני עמי
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means: if it is a secret, be silent and do not speak in the ears of those standing from my people.

sources.quote: ויאמר הס. שתוק עד שיצאו העומדים עלי
sources.says: Radak says it means be silent until those standing by me have gone out.

3:20.headline: 'A word of God' is why the king stands up
3:20.body: Rashi says a word of God means you must stand, and adds that for rising, Eglon earned Ruth as his descendant. Metzudat David says Ehud meant to keep him busy rising so he would not notice.

sources.quote: דְּבַר אֱלֹהִים לִי אֵלֶיךָ. וְצָרִיךְ אַתָּה לַעֲמוֹד
sources.says: Rashi says that on hearing 'a word of God to you', you must stand.

sources.quote: לְכָךְ זָכָה וְיָצְאָה מִמֶּנּוּ רוּת
sources.says: Rashi says that for this, Eglon merited that Ruth came from him.

sources.quote: וכונתו היה להטרידו בקימה לבל ירגיש
sources.says: Metzudat David says Ehud's aim was to keep him busy with standing up so he would not notice.

3:23.headline: The 'misdaron' is a porch set out in rows
3:23.body: מסדרון is used only here. Rashi gives Targum Jonathan's אכסדרא, a porch, and Metzudat Zion and Radak say it is named for סדר, order: a place laid out in rows of seats for those waiting for the king.

sources.quote: מִן הָעֲלִיָּה אֶל הַמִּסְדְּרוֹנָה, תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן: לְאַכְסַדְרָא
sources.says: Rashi says he went from the upper room to the corridor, and Targum Jonathan renders it אכסדרא.

sources.quote: היא האכסדרה המסודרת בכסאות לישיבת אנשים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the porch arranged with seats for people to sit.

sources.quote: והמסדרונ' מקום ישיבת העם הבאים אל המלך והמקום עשוי סדרים סדרים לשבת שם
sources.says: Radak says המסדרון is where the people who come to the king sit, a place made in rows for sitting.

3:24.headline: 'Covers his feet' is a polite way to say 'relieving himself'
3:24.body: Rashi gives Targum Jonathan's 'doing his needs', and Metzudat Zion says מסיך is a polite word for it, since a person sitting down covers his feet for modesty. Radak agrees that it is a respectful expression from סוכך, covering.

sources.quote: עָבֵיד צוֹרְכֵיהּ, הֵם נְקָבִים הַגְּדוֹלִים
sources.says: Rashi gives the Targum's 'doing his needs', meaning the large openings of the body.

sources.quote: על שם שדרך היושב להפנות, לסכך ולכסות רגליו מחמת צניעות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the name is because someone sitting to relieve himself covers his feet out of modesty.

sources.quote: ר״ל סוכך רגליו והוא לשון כבוד כלומר שהיה נפנה
sources.says: Radak says it means covering his feet, a respectful way of saying he was relieving himself.

3:26.headline: 'Until' here means 'while': Ehud escaped as they waited
3:26.body: עד usually means 'until', but Rashi, Metzudat Zion and Radak read it as 'while': Ehud escaped during their delay. Rashi compares it to 'until she wishes' in the Song of Songs, meaning while we both wish it.

sources.quote: אֶת הָאַהֲבָה עַד שֶׁתֶּחְפָּץ, בְּעוֹד שֶׁשְּׁנֵינוּ חֲפֵצִים בָּהּ
sources.says: Rashi compares it to 'until she desires', meaning while we both desire it.

sources.quote: עד. כמו בעוד
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says עד means 'while'.

sources.quote: עד התמהמהם. בעוד התמהמהם
sources.says: Radak says עד התמהמהם means while they were delaying.

3:26.headline: 'Seirathah': a thick wood, or just a place name?
3:26.body: Rashi says it is a dense wood, good for hiding, from thin branches that are called שער, 'hair'. Metzudat Zion and Radak say it is the name of a place.

sources.quote: יַעַר דַּק וְעָב, שֶׁקּוֹרִין ברוצ״ש בְּלַעַ״ז, וְטוֹב הוּא לְהֵחָבֵא
sources.says: Rashi says it is a thin and thick wood, good for hiding.

sources.quote: שֶׁעַנְפֵי אִילָנוֹת דַּקִּים קְרוּיִין שֵׂעָר
sources.says: Rashi says thin tree branches are called שער.

sources.quote: השעירתה. שם מקום
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says השעירתה is the name of a place.

sources.quote: והשעירתה. שם מקום
sources.says: Radak says השעירתה is the name of a place.

3:29.headline: 'Fat' Moabites: mighty, rich, or the choicest?
3:29.body: שמן means fat. Rashi gives Targum Jonathan's 'men of awe', and Radak and Ralbag read it as wealthy men, while Metzudat David says it means the choicest of them.

sources.quote: כָּל שָׁמֵן. (תרגום:) כָּל גְּבַר אֵימְתָן
sources.says: Rashi gives the Targum's 'every man of awe'.

sources.quote: ויש לפרש שמן עשירים וגדולים
sources.says: Radak says שמן can be explained as rich and great men.

sources.quote: כל שמן וכל איש חיל. ר״ל כל עשיר וכל גבור חיל
sources.says: Ralbag says it means every rich man and every mighty warrior.

sources.quote: כי בארץ ישראל היו כל המובחרים שבהם
sources.says: Metzudat David says that all the choicest of them were in the land of Israel.

3:31.headline: The ox-goad 'melamed' is named for teaching the ox
3:31.body: מלמד is used only here. Rashi calls it a goad, and Metzudat Zion and Radak say it is named from למד, 'teach', because the plowman uses it to teach the ox where to go.

sources.quote: מַלְמַד. הוּא דָּרְבָן, מַרְדֵּעַ
sources.says: Rashi says מלמד is a goad.

sources.quote: ובו מלמד ומורה הבקר לחרישה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says that with it he teaches and directs the ox in plowing.

sources.quote: נקרא כן כאלו מלמד הבקר לחרישה
sources.says: Radak says it is called this as if it teaches the ox to plow.

4:2.headline: Harosheth: a strong city, a craft town, or a forest?
4:2.body: Rashi says the city was named for being strong and ruling. Ralbag says it may be named for all the crafts done there, and Radak links the name to the Aramaic word for forest.

sources.quote: שֵׁם עִיר, עַל שֵׁם שֶׁהָיְתָה חֲזָקָה וְשׁוֹלֶטֶת
sources.says: Rashi says it is the name of a city, called so because it was strong and ruling.

sources.quote: כי לגודל העיר היתה נעשית שם כל המלאכה מהמלאכות אשר יעשו הגוים
sources.says: Ralbag says that because the city was so large, every kind of craft the nations practised was done there.

sources.quote: ופירוש חרושת הגוים מתרגמינן יער חרשא כי היו ביער ההוא מגדלים חזקים
sources.says: Radak says the Aramaic for forest is חרשא, and that strong towers stood in that forest.

4:3.headline: A louder cry than in the earlier stories
4:3.body: Earlier in the book Israel cries out with the word ויזעקו. Malbim says ויצעקו here is a stronger cry, because of the iron chariots, the harsh oppression, and the twenty long years.

sources.quote: ופה כתוב ויצעקו כי צעקה גדולה מזעקה
sources.says: Malbim says that here the verse writes ויצעקו, because a צעקה is a greater cry than a זעקה.

4:3.headline: Oppressed by force, or by insults?
4:3.body: בחזקה plainly means with strength, by force. Rashi cites Rabbi Tanchuma, who reads it as harsh, insulting words, as in Malachi 3:13, 'your words have been strong against Me'.

sources.quote: דָּרַשׁ רַבִּי תַּנְחוּמָא (צו ב): בְּגִדּוּפִין, וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר
sources.says: Rashi cites Rabbi Tanchuma, who reads 'with strength' as with insults, and brings a verse where strong words mean harsh speech.

sources.quote: דחק את ישראל בחוזק רב
sources.says: Metzudat David reads it plainly: he pressed Israel with great force.

4:4.headline: Lappidoth: Barak's other name, a wick-maker, or a fiery woman?
4:4.body: לפידות means torches. Radak says her husband was Barak, since torch and lightning are close in meaning, while Rashi says she made wicks for the Temple and Metzudat David says she acted quickly, like a flame.

sources.quote: אמרו שהוא ברק בן אבינועם וברק ולפידות קרובים בענין
sources.says: Radak says the sages identified Lappidoth with Barak son of Abinoam, since lightning and torches are close in meaning.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיְתָה עוֹשָׂה פְּתִילוֹת לַמִּקְדָּשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says she was called this because she made wicks for the Sanctuary.

sources.quote: אשת חיל, זריזה במעשיה כלפיד אש
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means a woman of valor, quick in her deeds like a flaming torch.

4:5.headline: Why Deborah judged under a palm tree
4:5.body: Metzudat David says she sat under an open tree so she was never alone with the men who came for judgment. Rashi, following the Targum, reads the verse as a list of her lands, starting with palm trees in Jericho.

sources.quote: לבל תתיחד עם האנשים הבאים אליה למשפט, קבעה ישיבתה תחת אילן תמר
sources.says: Metzudat David says she set her seat under a palm tree so she would not be alone with the men who came to her for judgment.

sources.quote: תְּמָרִים הָיוּ לָהּ בִּירִיחוֹ, וּכְרָמִים בָּרָמָה
sources.says: Rashi says she owned palm trees in Jericho and vineyards in Ramah.

4:6.headline: Which command does Deborah mean?
4:6.body: Rashi says she means the old command given through Moses, to destroy the Canaanites. Metzudat David says God told her this now in a prophecy, though the text does not record it.

sources.quote: בְּיַד מֹשֶׁה (דברים כ:יז): כִּי הַחֲרֵם תַּחֲרִימֵם
sources.says: Rashi says the command was given through Moses: you shall utterly destroy them.

sources.quote: באמת צוה ה׳, כי בנבואה נאמר לה, ועם שלא נזכר
sources.says: Metzudat David says God truly commanded it, told to her in prophecy, even though it is not written.

4:6.headline: Draw whom? Barak must win over frightened men
4:6.body: The verse says only 'draw' toward Mount Tabor, with no object. Radak and Metzudat David say Barak must draw the people with persuading words, because they feared Sisera's army.

sources.quote: תמשוך ישראל ותפתם בדברים עד שתביאם בהר תבור כי יראים היו מחיל סיסרא
sources.says: Radak says Barak must draw Israel and coax them with words until he brings them to Mount Tabor, because they feared Sisera's army.

sources.quote: משוך לבות בני ישראל לפתותם לבא עמך בהר תבור
sources.says: Metzudat David says Barak must draw the hearts of Israel and coax them to come with him to Mount Tabor.

4:7.headline: God would pull Sisera's heart toward the river
4:7.body: Radak says Sisera's star-gazers saw he would lose if he went out, but God drew his heart to go anyway. Metzudat David also reads it as God putting the wish in his heart.

sources.quote: אמר כי ראו אצטגניני סיסרא שלא יצא באותה מלחמה כי מנוצח יהיה אם יצא והקב"ה משך לבו לצאת
sources.says: Radak cites a saying that Sisera's astrologers saw he should not go to that battle because he would lose, and God drew his heart to go out.

sources.quote: אתן בלבו ללכת אל נחל קישון
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means: I will put it in his heart to go to the Kishon stream.

4:9.headline: Which woman will Sisera fall to: Deborah or Yael?
4:9.body: Metzudat David says it means Yael, who later kills him. Radak says Deborah means herself, and Malbim says both: Deborah starts Sisera's fall and Yael finishes it.

sources.quote: הלא סיסרא יומת על ידי אשה, והיא יעל אשת חבר הקיני
sources.says: Metzudat David says Sisera will be killed by a woman, Yael the wife of Heber the Kenite.

sources.quote: אלא פירושו כך אם אלך לא תהיה תפארתך כי על ידי תהיה התשועה
sources.says: Radak says it means that if Deborah goes, the glory will not be Barak's, because the rescue will come through her.

sources.quote: כל הענין יתיחס לאשה, אם תחלת מפלתו, שקיבוץ העם יהיה ע"י דבורה, אם סוף מפלתו ע"י יעל
sources.says: Malbim says the whole thing will be credited to a woman: the start of his fall to Deborah and the end of it to Yael.

4:10.headline: 'At his feet': his followers, on foot, or because of him?
4:10.body: Rashi and Metzudat David read ברגליו as the men who walked behind Barak. Malbim offers two other readings: the men came because of Barak, or Barak went on foot against nine hundred iron chariots.

sources.quote: וַיַּעַל בְּרַגְלָיו. עִמּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says 'at his feet' means with him.

sources.quote: עם הלוכו אחריו
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means the men who walked after him.

sources.quote: או כפשוטו שלא היה לו סוס ורכב נגד תשע מאות רכב ברזל
sources.says: Malbim says it may also mean, literally, that Barak had no horse or chariot against the nine hundred iron chariots.

4:11.headline: A place named for pools of water
4:11.body: Radak notes the word is written one way and read another, but either way it is a place name. Rashi and Radak follow the Targum's 'plain of pools', from בצעי המים, ponds that gather in the fields.

sources.quote: דומה שלקחוהו מן בצעי המים בדברי רז"ל שהם גבים מלאים מים בשדות
sources.says: Radak says the Targum seems to take it from the sages' word for water pools, hollows full of water in the fields.

sources.quote: מְקוֹם מֵישַׁר שֶׁל בְּצָעִים
sources.says: Rashi says it is a plain of marshes.

4:18.headline: A one-time word for a blanket, read as 'my name is here'
4:18.body: Rashi and Radak explain שמיכה as a thick, fringed blanket. Radak also cites Resh Lakish, who found no such object anywhere in Scripture and read it as שמי כה, 'my name is here', a sign that Sisera did not touch Yael.

sources.quote: תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן: בְּגוֹנְכָא
sources.says: Rashi says the Targum renders it as a kind of heavy blanket.

sources.quote: חזרנו בכל המקרא ולא מצאנו כלי ששמו שמיכה
sources.says: Radak cites Resh Lakish, who searched all of Scripture and found no object called שמיכה, and read it as 'my name is here', testifying that Sisera did not touch Yael.

4:20.headline: Sisera tells Yael 'stand' in the form used for a man
4:20.body: עמד here looks like a command to a man. Rashi says it means 'be strong like a man', while Radak and Malbim read it as the basic form 'to stand', used as a command.

sources.quote: זָרְזִי עַצְמֵךְ כְּזָכָר. וְיֵשׁ פּוֹתְרִים: ׳עֲמֹד׳, כְּמוֹ לַעֲמֹד
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'make yourself bold like a man', and that some read it as 'to stand'.

sources.quote: עמוד. מקור ויאמר אליה לעמוד פתח האהל
sources.says: Radak says it is the basic verb form: he told her to stand at the tent door.

sources.quote: ומלת עמוד מקור במקום ציווי
sources.says: Malbim says the word is the basic verb form used in place of a command.

4:21.headline: The temple of the head, named for its thin flesh
4:21.body: Metzudat Zion says רקה is the side of the upper face, the temple. It is named for how little flesh is there, as in Pharaoh's dream of cows 'thin of flesh'.

sources.quote: הוא צד גובה הפנים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the side of the upper face, named for the little flesh on it, like 'thin of flesh' in Genesis 41:19.

sources.quote: בְּרַקָּתוֹ. (תרגום:) בְּצִידְעֵיהּ
sources.says: Rashi says the Targum renders it as his temple.

4:21.headline: Not 'he flew' but 'he was worn out'
4:21.body: The same letters can mean 'he flew', as in Isaiah 6:6. Radak says the vowel here marks the other sense: Sisera was already tired, so he slept and did not feel the blow.

sources.quote: העין בפתח להבדיל בינו ובין ויעף אלי שהוא ענין אחר ופי' ויעף וכבר עיף
sources.says: Radak says the vowel under the ע sets this word apart from 'he flew to me', which is a different meaning; here it means he was already tired.

sources.quote: ויעף. ענין יגיעה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means weariness.

5:1.headline: Two singers, but the verb says 'she sang'
5:1.body: Deborah and Barak sing together, yet ותשר is singular and feminine. Radak says the verb follows Deborah because she was the heart of the deed, just as 'Miriam and Aaron spoke' uses a feminine verb.

sources.quote: לפי שדבורה עיקר המעשה כמו ותדבר מרים ואהרן
sources.says: Radak says the verb is feminine because Deborah was the main actor, like 'Miriam and Aaron spoke'.

5:2.headline: Taking revenge, or breaking loose?
5:2.body: Radak reads בפרע פרעות as 'when vengeance was taken', because the Aramaic for 'take revenge' uses this root. Rashi reads it as breaches that enemies broke into Israel. Malbim reads it as Israel itself running loose or growing weak.

sources.quote: בפרוע פרעות. בנקום נקמות, תרגום נקום נקמת איתפרע פורענותא
sources.says: Radak says it means taking revenge, since the Aramaic translation of 'take revenge' uses this word.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁבָּאוּ פְּרָצוֹת עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁפָּרְצוּ בָּהֶם אוֹיְבֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it means when breaches came on Israel, as their enemies broke in on them.

sources.quote: אם מצד שפרעו מוסר, אם מצד חולשתם
sources.says: Malbim says Israel was 'loose', either because they threw off discipline or because they were weak.

5:8.headline: Looks like 'bread', but here it means war
5:8.body: לחם usually means bread. Here it is the only place it means battle, from the same root as מלחמה, war: war came right to the city gates.

sources.quote: לחם. מלשון מלחמה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from 'war'.

sources.quote: אָז הֻזְקְקוּ לְמִלְחָמָה בְּשַׁעֲרֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi explains that then they were forced into war at their own gates.

5:10.headline: Judges on the bench, a road, or a town?
5:10.body: Rashi reads מדין as judges, who now dare to hold court in public. Radak cites the Masorah, which says the word has three senses in the Bible: a town, a road and judgment.

sources.quote: וְאוֹתָן שֶׁיּוֹשְׁבִין עַל מִדִּין, לְשׁוֹן דַּיָּנִים
sources.says: Rashi says those who sit on מדין are judges.

sources.quote: חד לשון קרתא וחד לשון ארחא וחד לשון דין
sources.says: Radak cites the Masorah: one use means a town, one a road, and one judgment.

5:11.headline: Archers, marching troops, or pebbles underfoot?
5:11.body: Radak reads מחצצים from חצים, arrows: the noise of archers at the wells. Rashi brings Menachem's view, troops lined up for battle. Rashi's own view is pebbles in the stream bed, whose crunch could give away the people drawing water.

sources.quote: מקול מחצצים. מקול יורה החצים
sources.says: Radak says it is the sound of those shooting arrows.

sources.quote: פָּתַר מְנַחֵם: עוֹרְכֵי מִלְחָמָה וְסוֹדְרֵי קְרָב
sources.says: Rashi reports that Menachem explained it as those who set up battle lines.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן אַבְנֵי חִלּוּקֵי הַנַּחַל
sources.says: Rashi says the word means the smooth stones of the stream bed.

5:12.headline: Why does Deborah need to be told 'wake up'?
5:12.body: Plainly, עורי is a call to sing with all her strength. Rashi brings the sages' reading: Deborah praised herself ('until I, Deborah, arose'), so the spirit of prophecy left her and she had to be roused.

sources.quote: מִפְּנֵי שֶׁנִּתְהַלְּלָה וְאָמְרָה (פסוק ז) עַד שַׁקַּמְתִּי דְּבוֹרָה, נִסְתַּלְּקָה הֵימֶנָּה רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ
sources.says: Rashi cites the rabbis: because she praised herself, saying 'until I Deborah arose', the holy spirit left her.

5:13.headline: Not 'went down' but 'ruled over'
5:13.body: ירד looks like 'went down'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it from רדה, to rule: the few survivors of Israel ruled over the mighty.

sources.quote: יָרַד - יִרְדֶּה, כְּמוֹ (ישעיהו מה:א) לְרַד לְפָנָיו גוֹיִם
sources.says: Rashi says ירד means 'will rule', as in 'to subdue nations before him'.

sources.quote: ירד. ענין ממשלה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means ruling.

5:14.headline: Your peoples, or dimmed like dying coals
5:14.body: בעממיך sounds like עמים, peoples. Rashi also hears עוממות, coals that have gone dim: Saul of Benjamin would dim Amalek like dying embers.

sources.quote: שֶׁיִּגְרְמֶנּוּ וִיעַמֵּם אוֹתוֹ כְּגֶחָלִים עוֹמְמוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says Saul would dim Amalek like coals that have gone dim, and also gives the reading 'with your forces'.

5:14.headline: Not a rod or a tribe, but a writer's pen
5:14.body: שבט usually means a staff or a tribe. Radak and Metzudat Zion say here it is a pen, as the Aramaic translation renders it: the scribes of Zebulun came to fight too.

sources.quote: שבט. העט וכן תירגם יונתן בקולמוס דספרא
sources.says: Radak says שבט here is a pen, as Targum Jonathan renders it 'with the scribe's quill'.

sources.quote: שבט. רוצה לומר, קולמוס
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means a quill.

5:17.headline: Dan did not live by the ships; he gathered into them
5:17.body: יגור usually means 'to dwell'. Metzudat Zion reads it as 'gathering'. Rashi says Dan loaded his wealth onto ships, ready to flee.

sources.quote: יגור. יאסף, כמו (תהלים נט ד) יגורו עלי עזים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means 'gathers', as in 'the mighty gather against me'.

sources.quote: וְכֵן דָּן הִכְנִיס מָמוֹנוֹ בִּסְפִינוֹת לַעֲמוֹד וְלִבְרוֹחַ
sources.says: Rashi says Dan put his money into ships, ready to run.

5:20.headline: The stars fought 'from their paths'
5:20.body: Rashi reads this to mean a star stretches from the sky down to the earth, so it could fight from where it stands. Malbim says מסלה is a road worn by use: the stars came by the path they had already taken to help Joshua.

sources.quote: רֹאשׁ הַכּוֹכָב בַּשָּׁמַיִם וְסוֹפוֹ בָּאָרֶץ
sources.says: Rashi says the star's head is in the sky and its end is on the earth.

sources.quote: כי זה גדר שם מסלה על דרך כבושה שהולכים עליה תמיד
sources.says: Malbim says מסלה means a beaten road that is walked all the time.

5:21.headline: The river swept them out like ash from a stove
5:21.body: גרפם appears only here. Rashi links it to the shovel that sweeps ash from the hearth, and Metzudat Zion to the Aramaic name of that shovel.

sources.quote: טֵאטֵם מִן הָעוֹלָם, כְּמַגְרֵפָה זוֹ שֶׁגּוֹרֶפֶת אֶת הָאֵפֶר מִן הַכִּירָה
sources.says: Rashi says the river swept them out of the world like a shovel sweeps ash from the stove.

sources.quote: היעיס תרגם אונקלוס מגרופיתא
sources.says: Metzudat Zion notes that Onkelos translates the altar shovels as מגרופיתא, from the same root.

5:21.headline: The 'river of old' that had made a promise long ago
5:21.body: קדומים appears only here. Rashi brings the Talmud's reading: the Kishon had pledged itself back in the days of Egypt. The Aramaic translation reads it as the river where miracles were done for Israel of old.

sources.quote: שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה עָרֵב לַיָּם עַל זֶה מִימוֹת מִצְרַיִם
sources.says: Rashi says the river became a guarantor to the sea for this from the days of Egypt, citing the Talmud.

sources.quote: נַחֲלָא דְאִתְעֲבִידוּ בֵיהּ נִסִין וּגְבוּרָן מִלְקַדְמֵין לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Targum Jonathan renders it 'the river in which miracles and mighty deeds were done for Israel of old'.

5:23.headline: Who was Meroz, a town, a star, or a man?
5:23.body: Radak says Meroz was a town near the battle that did not come to help. Rashi brings the Talmud's two views: some say it was a star, some say an important man.

sources.quote: אָמְרֵי לַהּ כּוֹכְבָא הֲוָה, וְאָמְרֵי לַהּ גַּבְרָא חֲשִׁיבָא הֲוָה
sources.says: Rashi cites the Talmud: some say Meroz was a star, and some say it was an important man.

sources.quote: אורו מרוז. שם עיר קרובה למקום המלחמה
sources.says: Radak says Meroz is the name of a town close to the battle.

5:25.headline: A bowl for nobles, or a cup for water?
5:25.body: Radak reads ספל אדירים as a big bowl that great men drink from. Rashi says water itself is called אדירים, 'mighty', as in the Song at the Sea, so it is a water cup.

sources.quote: בספל גדול ששותין בו גדולים ואדירים
sources.says: Radak says it is a large bowl that great and noble people drink from.

sources.quote: שֶׁהַמַּיִם נִקְרְאוּ ׳אַדִּירִים׳, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (שמות טו:י): בְּמַיִם אַדִּירִים
sources.says: Rashi says water is called אדירים, as in 'in the mighty waters'.

5:26.headline: A workman's hammer, or a hammer for the weary man?
5:26.body: The Aramaic translation reads עמלים as workmen: she took up a smith's hammer. Rashi reads it as the weary one, Sisera himself, worn out from flight.

sources.quote: וִימִינָא לְאַרְזַפְתָּא דְנַפְחִין
sources.says: Targum Jonathan renders it 'and her right hand to the smiths' hammer'.

sources.quote: סִיסְרָא, שֶׁהָיָה עָמֵל וְיָגֵעַ
sources.says: Rashi says the weary one is Sisera, who was worn out and tired.

5:28.headline: Sisera's mother spoke, wailed, or peered out?
5:28.body: ותיבב appears only here. Rashi gives three readings: she spoke; she wailed, which the Talmud uses to define the sound of the shofar; or, his own view, she gazed. Radak notes the Aramaic translation also reads it as looking.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן דִּבּוּר, כְּמוֹ (ישעיהו נז:יט) נִיב שְׂפָתַיִם וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ פֵּרְשׁוּהוּ (ראש השנה לג:) לְשׁוֹן גְּנִיחָה
sources.says: Rashi says it can mean speech, and that the rabbis read it as groaning, like the shofar's teruah.

sources.quote: ויונתן תרגם ואודיקה לשון הבטה
sources.says: Radak says Targum Jonathan renders it as looking.

5:30.headline: 'A womb, two wombs': the enemy's crude word for captive girls
5:30.body: Sisera's ladies picture the spoil: רחם רחמתים, a girl or two for each man. Metzudat Zion says they named the girls by the womb, as a term of contempt.

sources.quote: עלמה ושתי עלמות, וקראן בלשון בזיון, על שם הרחם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means a girl and two girls, called by the womb in a scornful way.

sources.quote: רחם רחמתים. נערה או שתי נערות
sources.says: Radak says it means a girl or two girls.

6:11.headline: The angel 'sat': angels don't sit, so he waited
6:11.body: ישב usually means sit. Radak says angels are never seen sitting, only standing. So here it means the angel stayed under the tree and waited until Gideon turned to him.

sources.quote: אינו ר"ל ישיבה כי אין נראים המלאכים בישיבה כי אם בעמידה
sources.says: Radak says it does not mean sitting, since angels are seen only standing.

sources.quote: אלא ר"ל נתעכב שם תחת האלה עד שיפנה אליו גדעון
sources.says: Radak says it means he lingered under the tree until Gideon would turn to him.

6:11.headline: Beating wheat in a winepress, to hide it
6:11.body: A גת is a winepress, where grapes are trodden, not a place for wheat. Radak says Gideon beat the wheat there with a stick, instead of threshing it with animals in the open, to hide it from Midian.

sources.quote: כמו דש אלא שהדישה בבהמות וחביטה במקל
sources.says: Radak says חבט is like threshing, except threshing is done with animals and חבט with a stick.

sources.quote: באותו גת היה חובט החטים
sources.says: Radak says the גת is where grapes are trodden, and in that winepress he was beating the wheat.

sources.quote: להניס. רצה לומר, להבריח ולהטמין
sources.says: Metzudat David says the aim was to hide the grain and get it away from Midian.

6:13.headline: The wonders his fathers told him: last night's Passover Hallel
6:13.body: Gideon asks where are the wonders 'our fathers told us'. Rashi and Radak bring a midrash that it was Passover: the night before, his father had read him the Hallel, 'When Israel went out of Egypt'.

sources.quote: פֶּסַח הָיָה, אָמַר לוֹ: אֶמֶשׁ הִקְרַנִי אַבָּא אֶת הַהַלֵּל
sources.says: Rashi says it was Passover, and Gideon said that last night his father read him the Hallel.

sources.quote: אמש קראנו את ההלל והיה אבי מקראני בצאת ישראל ממצרים
sources.says: Radak brings the same midrash: last night we read the Hallel, and my father read me 'When Israel went out of Egypt'.

6:14.headline: Who turned to Gideon: the angel, or God Himself?
6:14.body: The verse says 'the Lord turned to him', though an angel had been speaking. Rashi and Malbim say God Himself now spoke. Metzudat David says it still means the angel of the Lord.

sources.quote: הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעַצְמוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it was the Holy One Himself.

sources.quote: עד עתה דבר עמו המלאך, ועתה פנה ה' אליו בדבור נבואיי
sources.says: Malbim says until now the angel spoke with him, and now God turned to him in prophecy.

sources.quote: רצה לומר, מלאך ה׳
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means the angel of the Lord.

6:14.headline: 'Go in this strength of yours': which strength?
6:14.body: Rashi says it is the merit Gideon earned by speaking up for Israel when he asked where God's wonders were. Radak says it is new strength that God had just given him.

sources.quote: בְּכֹחַ הַזְּכוּת הַזֶּה שֶׁלִּמַּדְתָּ סָנֵגוֹרְיָא עַל בָּנַי
sources.says: Rashi says it means the strength of the merit Gideon earned by defending God's children.

sources.quote: פירוש בכח שהוסיף לו
sources.says: Radak says it means the strength God added to him.

6:15.headline: 'My lord' or 'my Lord'? Gideon does not yet know who he faces
6:15.body: אדני can address a man or God. Radak says Gideon meant a man, since he did not yet know this was an angel. The Targum Jonathan translates it as God's name.

sources.quote: לשון חול הוא כי עדיין לא ידע גדעון כי מלאך ה' הוא
sources.says: Radak says the word is ordinary, not holy, because Gideon did not yet know it was an angel.

sources.quote: ויונתן תרגם לשון קודש
sources.says: Radak notes that Targum Jonathan translated it as a holy name.

6:19.headline: Matzah on the table: it was Passover
6:19.body: Gideon bakes מצות, unleavened bread. Rashi says this shows it was Passover, the day the barley offering was waved. That is why, in the next chapter, a Midianite dreams of a barley loaf.

sources.quote: לָמַדְנוּ שֶׁפֶּסַח הָיָה, יוֹם תְּנוּפַת הָעוֹמֶר
sources.says: Rashi says we learn that it was Passover, the day of waving the Omer.

6:20.headline: Why the angel's title changes from 'Elohim' to 'the Lord'
6:20.body: In verse 20 he is 'the angel of Elohim'. In verse 21, when he accepts the offering, he is 'the angel of the Lord'. Malbim explains that a messenger alone may not receive an offering, only one in whom God Himself is present.

sources.quote: ולכן בזה לא קראו מלאך אלהים כי זובח לאלהים יחרם, רק מלאך ה'
sources.says: Malbim says that when the angel received the offering the verse calls him the angel of the Lord, not of Elohim, because sacrifice to anything but God is forbidden.

sources.quote: שם אלהים יבא גם על המלאך
sources.says: Malbim says the name Elohim can be used for an angel, while 'angel of the Lord' shows God dwells in him.

6:24.headline: An altar named 'The Lord is Peace'
6:24.body: Rashi says Gideon named the altar 'The Lord is our peace', after God told him 'Peace to you, you will not die'. Malbim notes the sages learned from here that Shalom is itself a name of God.

sources.quote: ה׳ הוּא שְׁלוֹמֵנוּ
sources.says: Rashi says the name means 'the Lord is our peace'.

sources.quote: גִּדְעוֹן לַמִּזְבֵּחַ
sources.says: Rashi says it was Gideon who gave the altar this name.

sources.quote: הכא שם גופיה אקרי שלום
sources.says: Malbim quotes the sages that here God's own name is called Shalom.

6:25.headline: A bull fattened seven years, as long as Midian ruled
6:25.body: Rashi, following the Targum, says the second bull had been fattened for idol worship for seven years. Malbim and Ralbag tie those seven years to the seven years of Midian's rule.

sources.quote: דְּאִיתְפַּטַּם שֶׁבַע שְׁנִין לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
sources.says: Rashi says it was fattened for seven years for idol worship.

sources.quote: ופטמוהו משך זמן ממשלת מדין שהיה שבע שנים
sources.says: Malbim says the townspeople vowed it to their idol and fattened it through the seven years of Midian's rule.

sources.quote: וזה יורה כי זה הטעות היה מעת התחלת השעבוד
sources.says: Ralbag says this shows the idol worship began when the oppression began.

6:28.headline: Taken apart, not smashed: what the townspeople got wrong
6:28.body: God told Gideon to tear down (הרס) Baal's altar. The townspeople say it was smashed (נתץ). Malbim says הרס means taking a building apart and נתץ means breaking each stone. Gideon reused the stones whole for God's altar, but they did not know it.

sources.quote: יש הבדל בין הריסה לנתיצה, ההורס יפרק הבנין, והנותץ שובר כל אבן לשברים
sources.says: Malbim says the one who tears down takes the building apart, while the one who smashes breaks every stone.

sources.quote: רק הם שלא ידעו שבנה מזבח מן האבנים האלה חשבו שנתץ ושבר
sources.says: Malbim says they did not know he built an altar from those stones, so they thought he had smashed them.

6:31.headline: 'Will you save Baal?' means 'will you avenge him?'
6:31.body: הושיע usually means to save. Rashi says here it means to take revenge, as when David spoke of avenging himself with his own hand. Joash mocks the crowd: does a god need you to avenge him?

sources.quote: תִּנְקְמוּ נִקְמָתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'will you take his revenge'.

sources.quote: וכי אתם תושיעון אותו, בתמיה
sources.says: Metzudat David says Joash asks this in amazement.

6:32.headline: Jerubbaal: 'Let Baal fight him', a name that mocks Baal
6:32.body: The verse explains the name: 'let Baal contend with him'. Ralbag says Joash named his son this way as a dare, as if praying Baal would fight him. Malbim says the name announced that Gideon had quarreled with Baal and rejected him.

sources.quote: והוא קרא שם בנו ירובעל לזאת הסבה כאילו הוא מתפלל שירב בו הבעל
sources.says: Ralbag says Joash named his son Jerubbaal as if praying that Baal would fight him.

sources.quote: קרא לו בשם זה שיש לומר מריבה עם הבעל והוא כופר בו
sources.says: Malbim says the name declares a quarrel with Baal and a denial of him.

sources.quote: יָרֶב בּוֹ. בְּגִדְעוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says 'let him contend with him' means with Gideon.

6:34.headline: God's spirit here is a spirit of courage
6:34.body: Rashi and the Targum say God's spirit here is a spirit of might. Malbim, citing Maimonides, calls it the first step of prophecy, when a person is moved to save a whole people. Ralbag adds it may also have been holy spirit.

sources.quote: רוּחַ ה׳. רוּחַ גְּבוּרָה
sources.says: Rashi says the spirit of the Lord means a spirit of might.

sources.quote: וְרוּחַ גְבוּרָא מִן קֳדָם יְיָ
sources.says: The Targum translates 'a spirit of might from before the Lord'.

sources.quote: הוא רוח גבורה, כמו שאמר המורה, המדרגה הראשונה מהנבואה
sources.says: Malbim says it is a spirit of might, which Maimonides calls the first level of prophecy.

sources.quote: ויתכן עוד ששרתה עליו רוח הקדש
sources.says: Ralbag says it is also possible that holy spirit rested on him.

6:38.headline: 'And it was so', but not all of it: dew never stops
6:38.body: Gideon asked for dew on the fleece and dry ground all around. Rashi says only the first part happened, because God has a covenant that dew is never held back. Malbim agrees.

sources.quote: לֹא נִתְקַיֵּם, שֶׁהַבְּרִית כְּרוּתָה לַטַּל שֶׁאֵינוֹ נֶעְצָר
sources.says: Rashi says the dry ground did not happen, because there is a covenant that dew is never withheld.

sources.quote: כי ברית כרותה לטל בל יעצר
sources.says: Malbim says the verse leaves out the dry ground because there is a covenant for dew not to be held back.

6:39.headline: Testing God is forbidden, so what was Gideon testing?
6:39.body: The Torah says 'do not test the Lord'. Radak, citing Saadia, says Gideon did not doubt God's power. He was testing whether he himself was worthy of so great a miracle.

sources.quote: והנה כתיב לא תנסו את ה'
sources.says: Radak raises the problem that the Torah forbids testing God.

sources.quote: אבל גדעון לא היה לו ספק ביכולת הבורא אלא רצה לנסות אם הוא ראוי לנס גדול כזה
sources.says: Radak says Gideon did not doubt God's power; he wanted to test whether he was worthy of such a miracle.

7:1.headline: Givat HaMoreh, the hill of watching and pointing
7:1.body: Moreh comes from the word for pointing out. Rashi says lookouts on this hill watched the valley and signaled into it, and Radak says a watchman may have pointed out the roads from there.

sources.quote: הַמּוֹרֶה, לְשׁוֹן הוֹרָאָה וּרְאִיָּה, כְּמוֹ (משלי ו:יג) מוֹרֶה בְּאֶצְבְּעוֹתָיו, שֶׁמִּשָּׁם צוֹפִים וְרוֹמְזִים בָּעֵמֶק
sources.says: Rashi says moreh means pointing and seeing, as in 'points with his fingers' in Proverbs 6:13, because from there they watch and signal into the valley.

sources.quote: ואפשר שהיה שם צופה מורה הדרכים
sources.says: Radak says there may have been a lookout there who pointed out the roads.

7:3.headline: Leave at dawn, circle away, or fly off like birds
7:3.body: Rashi reads ויצפר from the Aramaic צפרא, morning, so the fearful should slip home at dawn. Radak also suggests 'circle away', like a wrapped turban, and Malbim hears צפור, bird: they would later fly after the enemy.

sources.quote: בַּבֹּקֶר, לְשׁוֹן אֲרָמִי: צַפְרָא
sources.says: Rashi says it means in the morning, from the Aramaic word tzafra.

sources.quote: או פי' יסבב כלומר יסוב מהר הגלעד וישוב לו וכן נקראת המצנפת צפירה לפי שסובבים אותה על הראש
sources.says: Radak says it may instead mean to go around and turn back from Mount Gilead, as a turban is called tzefirah because it is wound around the head.

sources.quote: ועל זה אמר לשון יצפור, שמורה ג״כ שיעופו מהר כצפרים עפות אחר האויב
sources.says: Malbim says the word also hints that they would fly quickly, like birds, after the enemy.

7:4.headline: God will refine the troops the way a smith refines silver
7:4.body: צרף is the word for smelting metal. Metzudat David and Radak say God will separate the people like dross from silver, so that only the righteous go to this war.

sources.quote: אעשה כהצורף הזה, המפריד הסיגים מן הכסף
sources.says: Metzudat David says God will act like a smith who separates the dross from the silver.

sources.quote: כמו שצורפין הכסף מהסיגים שלא יהיה במלחמה ההיא רק הצדיקים
sources.says: Radak says it is like refining silver from dross, so that only the righteous fight in that war.

7:5.headline: Lapping like a dog, yet drinking from the hand
7:5.body: This verse says they lapped with the tongue like a dog, but the next says they lapped from their hands. Metzudat David says one who scoops water in his hands cannot sip with his lips, so he licks it with his tongue, as a dog does.

sources.quote: כי השואב את המים בתוך ידיו ושותה מהם, אי אפשר לו לשתות בשפתיו כדרך כל הארץ רק מלקק בלשונו כדרך שתיית הכלב
sources.says: Metzudat David says one who drinks water from his hands cannot drink with his lips, only lick with his tongue the way a dog drinks.

sources.quote: ענין לחיכה בלשון, כמו (מלכים א כא יט) ילקו הכלבים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means licking with the tongue, as in 'the dogs shall lick' in 1 Kings 21:19.

7:9.headline: 'Into the camp' means attack; 'to the camp' means spy
7:9.body: God first tells Gideon to go down 'into' the camp, then, if he is afraid, 'to' the camp. Malbim says 'into' means falling on it to conquer it, while 'to' means standing at a distance to hear what they say.

sources.quote: במחנה, הוא שיפול במחנה לכבשה, ואל המחנה, הוא שיעמוד מרחוק לשמוע מה ידברו
sources.says: Malbim says 'into the camp' means to fall on it and conquer it, and 'to the camp' means to stand at a distance and hear what they say.

7:13.headline: A roasted barley cake, or the sound of one rolling
7:13.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion say צליל is a cake roasted on coals. Radak and Ralbag also read it as a sound, as in 'ears will tingle', so the man heard the barley bread rumbling through the camp.

sources.quote: מלשון צלי, ורצונו לומר חררה אפויה על הגחלים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from the word for roasting and means a cake baked on coals.

sources.quote: חֲרָרָה שֶׁאוֹפִין עַל הַגֶּחָלִים
sources.says: Rashi, following the Targum, says it is a cake baked on coals.

sources.quote: והוא מענין תצילנה אזניו כלומר שמע רעש לחם שעורים
sources.says: Radak says it may come from 'his ears will tingle', meaning he heard the noise of the barley bread, or from roasting.
